chunks: "At steady state the current isn't changing, so the inductor drops no voltage and the winding is basically its resistance, plus the back-EMF for a motor. There are two extremes.
Maximum current is the stalled case: the shaft isn't turning, so there's no back-EMF, the current is V over R, and the torque is at its maximum.
Nothing moves, so no mechanical power is produced and all the electrical power, V squared over R, goes into heating the winding.
With 12 volts and 1 ohm that's 12 amps and 144 watts into a few tens of grams of copper, which heats at tens of degrees per second, so it burns out in seconds if you don't limit it.
The magnetic field is at its strongest too, storing half L I squared. Minimum current is free-running with no load.
The motor is at its highest speed, the back-EMF is nearly equal to the supply, and the current is just enough to overcome friction, maybe half an amp.
Almost all the input power goes to friction and windage, not useful work, so efficiency is zero there too. Efficiency peaks somewhere in between.
For a solenoid it's the same logic: steady state is just V over R, held current, with all the power as heat, unless you reduce the voltage after pull-in."
